0.title: Understanding People, Sharing the Gospel
0.essay:
The gospel never changes. People do. The same good news that Peter preached to Jews in Jerusalem, Paul reasoned through with philosophers in Athens and Philip explained to an Ethiopian official on a desert road reaches each of us where we actually are. This short study is about learning to see people as they are, so that we can speak the unchanging gospel to them with understanding and love.

Why understanding matters

Paul’s preaching in Acts never sounds the same twice. In the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch he begins with Israel’s history and the promises to David (Acts 13). In Lystra, among farmers who had never read the Scriptures, he speaks of the God who gives “rains from heaven and fruitful seasons” (Acts 14:17). In Athens he quotes their own poets (Acts 17:28). The message is the same — Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, Lord and Saviour — but he starts from different places, because his hearers started from different places. “I have become all things to all people,” he says, “that by all means I might save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22).

Understanding someone is a form of love. When we take the trouble to learn what a person believes, what they hope for and what troubles them, we treat them as a person made in God’s image rather than a target. And we are far more likely to say something that actually reaches them.

How each chapter works

Ten chapters look at ten kinds of people a Christian is likely to meet. Two are at home in the modern West: the secular Westerner and the person who is “spiritual but not religious”. Three come from a Christian background: Roman Catholics, who share the historic creeds but differ on how a sinner is made right with God; and Jehovah’s Witnesses and Latter-day Saints, who use Christian words with very different meanings. And five belong to the world’s other great faiths: friends who are Jewish, Muslim, Hindu, Sikh or Buddhist. Each chapter moves in three steps.

Who they are. What do they believe? What do they strive for, and what do they value most? What are their big questions, and where are they uneasy or unsatisfied? And why do they see the world as they do — what history, culture and experience have shaped them?

What the Bible says to them. Which truths of Scripture speak most directly into their situation — both to meet their deepest longings and to correct where they go wrong?

Where to begin. How can an ordinary Christian start a real conversation — what to ask, what to avoid, and how to bring Christ in naturally?

A final chapter brings it together in the gospel conversation itself: how to listen, ask good questions and explain the good news clearly.

A word of caution

No one is a category. A Jewish friend may be devout or entirely secular; a Muslim colleague may pray five times a day or never; a Catholic friend may trust Christ alone more than they realise; a “secular” neighbour may be quietly searching. What follows describes common patterns, not boxes to put people in. Always let the person in front of you tell you who they are.

Remember, too, that no technique converts anyone. “No one can come to me,” said Jesus, “unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). Our part is to pray, to love, to live faithfully and to speak the truth clearly and gently. God’s part is to give life. That frees us from pressure, and it keeps us praying.

And finally, the best evangelism usually happens in ordinary friendship. Peter tells believers to be “prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15). People ask about our hope when they have seen it. So be a good friend, a good neighbour and a good colleague — and be ready.

1.title: The Secular Westerner
1.essay:
Most people we meet in the West are not committed atheists with a worked-out philosophy. They have simply grown up in a world where God is optional. They are not hostile to Christianity so much as unfamiliar with it — and quietly unsure whether life means anything at all.

Who they are

The secular Westerner usually assumes, without ever having decided it, that the natural world is all there is. Science explains how things work; anything beyond that is private opinion. Religion is a personal preference, like taste in music: fine if it helps you, but not something that can be true or false for everyone. They are suspicious of anyone who claims to know the truth about God, because such claims seem arrogant and divisive.

What they value most is the freedom to be themselves. The philosopher Charles Taylor calls this the age of authenticity: the highest calling is to discover who you really are and to live it out, without letting family, religion or tradition tell you who to be. The great virtues are tolerance, kindness, fairness and being true to yourself. The great sins are judging, excluding and imposing your views on others. Many care deeply about justice — about racism, poverty, the environment, the vulnerable — and they are often more generous than they give themselves credit for.

They strive for a good life: meaningful work, close relationships, experiences, wellbeing, a sense that their life counts. But underneath, there is often unease. The promise that you can create your own meaning turns out to be heavy. If my identity is something I must build, then I can fail at it — and many young people are anxious, lonely and exhausted from trying. Social media turns life into a performance. Success does not satisfy for long. And death, which the culture rarely talks about, remains unanswered.

Their big questions are seldom “Does God exist?” in the abstract. They are more personal. Who am I? Does my life matter? Why do I feel so empty when I have so much? What is the right thing to do, and why? How can I live with what I have done? What happens when I die? Many also carry a question shaped by suffering: if there is a God, why does he allow so much pain?

Why they see the world this way. The West has spent several centuries learning to explain the world without God. The Enlightenment trusted human reason to find truth on its own; science brought extraordinary progress, and with it the sense that what cannot be measured is not quite real. Prosperity and technology made life more comfortable and God seem less necessary. The church has also, at times, given people reason to distrust it — through scandal, hypocrisy or a faith that seemed to have nothing to say to real life. So for many, Christianity is not something they rejected after careful thought; it is simply something they never really encountered, or encountered only in caricature.

Yet the secular Westerner has not escaped the questions God placed in the human heart. They still believe that people have dignity, that injustice is truly wrong, that love is more than chemistry, that beauty matters. Those convictions came, historically, from Christianity — and they make little sense without it.

What the Bible says to them

You are made, not self-made. The deepest answer to “Who am I?” is that you were created by God, in his image (Genesis 1:27). Your worth is not something you have to earn or construct; it was given. This is wonderful news for people worn out by the demand to make themselves. It also explains why they cannot shake their sense that people matter and justice is real: they are reflecting the image of the God who made them.

Your longing points somewhere. “He has put eternity into man’s heart” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). The book of Ecclesiastes reads like a modern secular memoir: a man who tried work, pleasure, wealth and wisdom, and found them all “vanity” — vapour — when cut off from God. The restlessness so many feel is not a malfunction. Augustine prayed, “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” Jesus offers what nothing else can: “I came that they may have life and have it abundantly” (John 10:10).

The problem is deeper than we think. Secular culture tends to see people as basically good, held back by bad systems or poor self-esteem. The Bible is more honest. The trouble is not out there but in here: we have turned from God and put ourselves at the centre (Romans 1:21–25). That is why the self cannot bear the weight we put on it, and why our best efforts at justice are always mixed with pride. Sin is not a word people like, but it names something they recognise: the gap between who they want to be and who they are.

There is real forgiveness. Our culture is quick to condemn and has little to offer the guilty — only shaming or excusing. The gospel offers something no secular philosophy can: guilt honestly faced and fully forgiven, because Christ bore it. “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). For people haunted by what they have done, or by never measuring up, this is life-changing.

Truth is a person, and he rose. Christianity is not first a set of values or a private preference. It rests on events in history: the life, death and resurrection of Jesus. “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). That makes Christianity open to investigation, which secular people respect. And the resurrection answers the question the culture avoids: death is not the end.

Where to begin

Be curious about their life. Ask real questions and listen to the answers. What gives your life meaning? What are you hoping for? What do you think makes a good life? Most people are rarely asked such questions, and many are glad to talk. You will learn where their hopes and their unease lie.

Gently explore their convictions. Many secular people hold beliefs that their worldview cannot support. If someone says that every person matters, or that some things are truly evil, you can ask with genuine interest: “Where do you think that comes from? If we are just the product of chance, why would people have dignity?” This is not a trap but an invitation to see that their deepest convictions point beyond the world they assume. Tim Keller called these “clues” to God.

Do not start with arguments for God’s existence. Unless they are interested in philosophy, begin with life rather than theory: meaning, identity, guilt, suffering, death, love. Share honestly how faith in Christ has changed how you face these things. Your story is not proof, but it is evidence that the gospel is livable.

Invite them to look at Jesus. Many have never read a Gospel. Suggest reading Mark or Luke together, or offer them a copy and ask what they make of it. Jesus himself is far more compelling than our arguments. Let them meet him.

Live a life that raises questions. In a lonely culture, Christian community is powerful: genuine friendship, hospitality, care for the poor, forgiveness, joy in suffering. Invite friends into your home before you invite them to church. Jesus said, “By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

Be patient. Secular people often come to faith slowly, over months or years, through many conversations and relationships. Pray for them by name. Keep the friendship whether or not they show interest. God is at work long before we see it.

2.title: Spiritual but Not Religious
2.essay:
“I’m spiritual, but not religious.” It may be the most common description of faith in the West today. The people who say it are not closed to God — often quite the opposite. They sense there is more to life than the material world. What they distrust is organised religion: its rules, its institutions and its claims to have the truth.

Who they are

The spiritual-but-not-religious person believes in something beyond the physical — God, a higher power, the universe, energy, the divine within. Their spirituality is personal and self-directed. They may meditate or practise yoga, use crystals or tarot cards, follow astrology, speak of manifesting what they want, keep a gratitude journal, feel close to the sacred in nature, or borrow freely from Buddhism, Hinduism, Indigenous traditions and Christianity. Each person assembles their own spiritual path, taking what resonates and leaving the rest.

What they value most is authenticity, freedom and inner experience. Spirituality, for them, is about how you feel and who you are becoming, not about doctrines or institutions. They want peace, balance, healing and personal growth. Many speak of “energy” and “vibes”, of the universe sending signs, of everything happening for a reason. They tend to believe that all religions point to the same truth, that the divine is found within us, and that love and kindness are what really matter.

Their big questions are often about the self and its wellbeing. How can I find peace? How can I heal from my past? What is my purpose? Is the universe guiding me? How do I become my best self? Underneath, there may be real uncertainty. A spirituality you build for yourself can feel fragile when tragedy strikes. If the divine is within me, what happens when I find darkness within? If the universe rewards positive energy, what does my suffering say about me? And many feel lonely: a spirituality of one has no community to hold you.

Why they see the world this way. Many grew up with little religion, or with a religion that felt cold, judgmental or hypocritical. Some were hurt by churches. They inherited secular culture’s suspicion of authority and its belief that each person must find their own truth, but they could not accept that the material world is all there is. Their hearts told them otherwise. The wellness industry, social media and a flood of spiritual products offer endless options. The result is a consumer spirituality: personal, flexible and centred on the self.

Behind this lies something true. They are right that human beings are more than matter, right to long for transcendence, right to sense that life is meant to be meaningful. They are responding, however confusedly, to the God who “has put eternity into man’s heart” (Ecclesiastes 3:11).

What the Bible says to them

Your hunger is real — and points to a person. The Bible affirms the spiritual longing these friends feel. Paul told the spiritual seekers of Athens that God made us “that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us” (Acts 17:27). But the One we long for is not an energy or a force; he is a personal God who knows us by name and has spoken.

God is not within us — he comes to us. A spirituality that looks inward for the divine will eventually meet our own darkness. The Bible is honest: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick” (Jeremiah 17:9). We do not need to discover a god within; we need the true God to come from outside and make us new. That is exactly what he has done in Jesus.

The universe is not in charge; a Father is. Many speak of the universe guiding them. The Bible speaks of something far better: a loving heavenly Father who governs all things, who knows what we need before we ask (Matthew 6:8), and who works even suffering for the good of his children (Romans 8:28). He is not manipulated by our thoughts or energy. He is trusted.

Not all paths are the same. It sounds humble to say all religions lead to the same place, but it actually ignores what they teach — they contradict one another on the most basic questions. Jesus made a claim no spiritual teacher can share: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). He is not one option on a spiritual menu, but the One the whole menu is searching for.

Grace, not self-improvement. Self-made spirituality is exhausting: always growing, healing, raising your vibration. The gospel brings rest. “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Peace with God is not an achievement but a gift, because Christ has done what we could not.

Belonging, not just believing. God does not save isolated spiritual consumers but brings people into a family. The church, for all its flaws, is “the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19), where the lonely find a home.

Where to begin

Take their spirituality seriously. Do not mock crystals or astrology. Ask with real interest: What does spirituality mean to you? What practices help you? Have you ever had an experience you could only call spiritual? You will learn what they are seeking.

Share your own spiritual life. Talk about prayer, about times you have known God’s presence, about how he has met you in hard times. Many spiritual seekers are surprised that Christians have a living relationship with God rather than just rules.

Gently ask the deeper questions. Who or what do you think the divine is? Can a force love you? How do you deal with the darkness inside yourself? What happens if the universe does not give you what you manifest? These questions open the way to a personal God and to grace.

Acknowledge church hurt. If they have been wounded by Christians, listen and apologise where it is right. Show them that Jesus himself was hardest on religious hypocrisy and kindest to the hurting and the outsider.

Introduce them to Jesus himself. Many have a vague, positive view of Jesus as a spiritual teacher. Suggest reading John’s Gospel together, with its language of light, life and spirit. Let them meet the real Jesus, who is both gentler and more demanding than they expect.

Offer community. Invite them into your life, your home and your church family. For people who have built a spirituality alone, the warmth of real Christian community can be the most powerful witness of all.

3.title: Roman Catholic Friends
3.essay:
Roman Catholics are our neighbours, colleagues and often our relatives. Many love Jesus and share with us belief in the Trinity, the deity of Christ, his virgin birth, death and resurrection. Some are devout believers; many others are Catholic in name only. Speaking with Catholic friends is less about introducing a new God than about the most important question of all: how is a sinner made right with God?

Who they are

The Roman Catholic Church is the largest Christian body in the world, with well over a billion members. It traces its authority back to the apostle Peter and teaches that the pope, as Peter’s successor, is the head of the church on earth. Authority, for Catholics, rests on Scripture and Tradition together, interpreted by the church’s teaching office, the Magisterium.

Catholics confess the historic creeds. They believe in one God in three persons, that Jesus Christ is fully God and fully man, that he died for sinners and rose again, and that he will return to judge. These are great shared truths, and Christians from the Reformation tradition should rejoice in them.

Catholic spiritual life is centred on the seven sacraments: baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist (the Mass), penance (confession), anointing of the sick, marriage and holy orders. Catholics believe that in the Mass the bread and wine become the actual body and blood of Christ (transubstantiation), and that the Mass is a re-presentation of Christ’s sacrifice. Grace is received especially through the sacraments, beginning with baptism, which is taught to wash away original sin and give new life. Mary is honoured as the Mother of God, free from sin, taken bodily into heaven, and a powerful intercessor; Catholics also pray to the saints for their help.

Catholic teaching holds that justification is a process: grace is poured into the soul, and we cooperate with it, growing in holiness through faith, love, good works and the sacraments. Mortal sin can destroy grace, which is restored through confession. Those who die in God’s grace but not fully purified pass through purgatory before entering heaven. Because of this, most Catholics believe it would be presumptuous to be sure of their salvation.

Catholics are hugely varied. Some are devout and well taught, some are evangelical in their love for Scripture, some are traditionalists who love the old Latin Mass, many are cultural Catholics who attend only at Christmas or for weddings and funerals. Their big questions often include: Am I good enough for God? How can I be sure I will go to heaven? Why do I still feel guilty after confession? What does the church really teach, and why? Some have been shaken by abuse scandals in the church.

Why they see the world this way. For many Catholics, the church is family, culture and identity, inherited from parents and grandparents. Its beauty, history and sense of the sacred are deeply attractive. Its structure of priests, sacraments and saints gives a sense of God’s presence and help. And they may have been taught that Protestants broke away from the true church and invented a cheap, easy faith. Leaving the Catholic church can feel like betraying family and heritage.

What the Bible says to them

Justification is a gift, received by faith alone. This was the heart of the Reformation, and it remains the heart of the matter. Scripture teaches that God declares sinners righteous not because of anything in them, but because of Christ’s righteousness credited to them, received through faith: “to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness” (Romans 4:5). Good works follow as fruit, never as the ground of our acceptance. “By grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9).

Christ’s sacrifice is finished. The Mass presents Christ’s sacrifice as continually offered. Hebrews insists that Christ “has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Hebrews 9:26), and that “by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). On the cross he said, “It is finished” (John 19:30). Nothing needs to be added or repeated.

Assurance is God’s will for his children. Catholic teaching discourages certainty of salvation. But Scripture invites it, because salvation rests on Christ’s work, not ours: “I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13). “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). There is no purgatory still to pay for sins, because Christ’s blood “cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7).

One mediator. We need no other intercessor than Christ: “There is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). He invites us to come directly to the Father in his name. Mary herself pointed away from herself to her Son: “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5).

Scripture is the final authority. Tradition can be valuable, but it must be tested by God’s word. Jesus rebuked the religious leaders of his day for “making void the word of God by your tradition” (Mark 7:13). Scripture is God-breathed and sufficient to equip us “for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

Where to begin

Start with what you share. Affirm the great truths you hold in common: the Trinity, the deity of Christ, his death and resurrection. Do not treat your Catholic friend as a pagan. Many Catholics truly trust Christ, sometimes more than they realise.

Ask about assurance. One of the most helpful questions is simple: “If you died tonight, are you sure you would be with God? Why?” Listen carefully. The answer usually shows whether your friend is trusting in Christ alone or in their own efforts and the sacraments.

Talk about grace, not just the institution. Avoid getting drawn into arguments about the pope, Mary or church history at first. Focus on the gospel itself: what Christ has done, and how we receive it. Share how you came to know that you are accepted because of Christ alone.

Read the Bible together. Many Catholics are encouraged to read Scripture but rarely do. Romans, Galatians and Hebrews speak directly to the questions of justification and Christ’s finished work. Read a chapter together and ask, “What does this say about how we are saved?”

Be gracious and patient. Catholics may have heard Protestants speak harshly about their church. Speak with respect and love. Change, if it comes, may take time, and leaving the Catholic church can be painful for families. Pray that God would give your friend the joy and assurance of resting in Christ alone.

4.title: Jehovah’s Witnesses
4.essay:
Jehovah’s Witnesses are best known for knocking on doors. Most Christians close the door as quickly as they can. But Witnesses are often sincere, disciplined people who want to serve God — and they are one of the few groups who come looking for a conversation about the Bible. That is an opportunity worth taking.

Who they are

The movement began in the 1870s in Pennsylvania, when Charles Taze Russell started a Bible study group that came to reject many traditional Christian teachings. It grew into the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society, and in 1931 took the name Jehovah’s Witnesses, from Isaiah 43:10. Today there are some eight and a half million active Witnesses worldwide. They are led by a small Governing Body at their headquarters in New York, which Witnesses regard as God’s channel of truth on earth.

Witnesses believe that Jehovah alone is the true God. They deny the Trinity, which they consider a pagan idea. Jesus, they teach, is God’s first creation, the archangel Michael before his human life — “a god”, but not God Almighty. The Holy Spirit is not a person but God’s active force. Jesus died on a stake, not a cross, and was raised as a spirit, not in his body. They do not believe in an immortal soul or in hell; the wicked will simply cease to exist.

They teach that only 144,000 “anointed” believers will reign with Christ in heaven; the rest of the faithful hope to live for ever in a restored paradise on earth after Armageddon, the coming battle in which God will destroy the wicked. Salvation depends on faith in Jesus’ ransom, but also on faithful obedience: attending meetings, preaching door to door, living by the organisation’s rules, and remaining loyal to it. They use their own translation of the Bible, the New World Translation, which renders key verses differently from other Bibles, most famously John 1:1, “the Word was a god.”

Witness life is highly organised and demanding. Members attend several meetings a week at the Kingdom Hall, study Watchtower publications, and spend many hours in preaching work. They do not celebrate birthdays or Christmas, salute flags, vote or join the military, and they refuse blood transfusions, even at risk of death. Those who leave or are expelled (“disfellowshipped”) are often shunned by family and friends who remain.

What Witnesses strive for is to be faithful to Jehovah and to survive Armageddon into paradise. Their big questions, often unspoken, include: Am I doing enough? Will I be found faithful? What if the organisation is wrong? Many live with a quiet anxiety about whether they measure up, and some carry deep questions they are afraid to voice.

Why they see the world this way. Many Witnesses were raised in the faith; others joined because they found warmth, structure and clear answers when traditional churches seemed vague or hypocritical. They are taught that all other churches belong to “false religion”, that outside information is dangerous, and that doubting the Governing Body is doubting God. Leaving can mean losing family, friends and community at once — a very high cost.

What the Bible says to them

Jesus is God. This is the central issue. John 1:1 in the original Greek says, “the Word was God” — as virtually every translation renders it. Thomas worshipped the risen Jesus as “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28), and Jesus accepted it. Hebrews says the Father himself calls the Son God (Hebrews 1:8) and commands the angels to worship him (Hebrews 1:6) — something no created angel could rightly receive. Isaiah calls the coming child “Mighty God” (Isaiah 9:6), the same title Witnesses rightly give to Jehovah (Isaiah 10:21).

Jesus is Jehovah. The New Testament takes Old Testament passages about Jehovah and applies them to Jesus. Isaiah says every knee will bow to Jehovah (Isaiah 45:23); Paul says every knee will bow to Jesus (Philippians 2:10–11). Jesus took God’s own name: “Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58), and his hearers understood the claim, picking up stones to stone him for blasphemy.

The Spirit is a person. The Holy Spirit speaks (Acts 13:2), teaches (John 14:26), can be grieved (Ephesians 4:30) and lied to — and lying to him is lying to God (Acts 5:3–4). A force does not do these things.

Salvation is by grace, with assurance. Witnesses work hard to remain faithful, with no certainty they will be found acceptable. The gospel offers rest: “For by grace you have been saved through faith… not a result of works” (Ephesians 2:8–9). And it offers assurance: “Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life” (John 5:24).

Christ, not an organisation. Jesus said, “Come to me” (Matthew 11:28), not to an organisation. Every believer can know God personally through him, read his word for themselves, and be led by his Spirit. There is “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

Where to begin

Open the door — and be kind. Witnesses are used to rejection. Simple kindness — inviting them in, offering a drink, listening — can make a deep impression. Remember that they are people, often under great pressure, not just opponents in an argument.

Know a few key passages well. You do not need to answer every point. Focus on who Jesus is: John 1:1–3, John 8:58, John 20:28, Hebrews 1, Colossians 1:15–20 and Philippians 2:5–11. Ask them to read the verses aloud and explain them. Compare their translation with others, kindly.

Ask questions that invite reflection. “Do you know that you will be saved?” “What does Jesus mean to you personally?” “If the Governing Body taught something that seemed to contradict the Bible, what would you do?” Questions are more effective than lectures, and plant seeds that may grow later.

Share the joy of grace. Tell them how you know God accepts you, not because of your performance but because of Christ. Many Witnesses have never heard a Christian speak of assurance with joy.

Be ready for a long journey. Witnesses are trained to resist and usually visit in pairs, which makes honest discussion harder. Change, if it comes, often takes years — and leaving costs them dearly. If a Witness begins to question, be a faithful friend; they may lose everyone else. Pray for them by name after they leave your doorstep.

5.title: Mormon Friends (Latter-day Saints)
5.essay:
Latter-day Saints are often among the friendliest, most family-centred and morally serious people you will meet. They speak of Jesus, Heavenly Father, grace and the atonement, and many consider themselves Christians. Yet behind the familiar words lies a very different understanding of God, Christ and salvation. Loving them well means understanding both.

Who they are

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints was founded by Joseph Smith in New York State in 1830. Smith taught that as a teenager he saw God the Father and Jesus Christ in a vision, and was told that all existing churches were wrong. He said that an angel, Moroni, later led him to golden plates, which he translated as the Book of Mormon — an account of ancient peoples in the Americas whom Christ visited after his resurrection. After persecution and Smith’s death in 1844, most followers went west under Brigham Young and settled in Utah. Today the church has some seventeen million members worldwide.

Latter-day Saints accept the Bible “as far as it is translated correctly”, alongside the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants and the Pearl of Great Price. They are led by a president regarded as a living prophet, who can receive new revelation for the church.

Their teaching about God is very different from historic Christianity. They believe God the Father has a glorified physical body and was once a man who progressed to godhood. The Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost are three separate beings, united in purpose. Human beings lived as spirit children of Heavenly Parents before birth, and through obedience can progress toward becoming like God themselves (exaltation). Jesus is the firstborn spirit child of the Father, our elder brother, who atoned for sin in Gethsemane and on the cross.

Salvation in their teaching has several levels. Almost everyone will be resurrected and enter one of three “kingdoms of glory”. But the highest, exaltation in the celestial kingdom with God and one’s family for ever, requires faith, repentance, baptism, temple ordinances such as eternal marriage, and lifelong obedience to the church’s commandments. A famous verse in the Book of Mormon says we are saved by grace “after all we can do” (2 Nephi 25:23). Members tithe ten per cent, observe a health code (no alcohol, tobacco, coffee or tea), serve missions as young people, and perform baptisms on behalf of the dead in their temples. In recent decades many Latter-day Saint leaders have spoken more warmly of grace, but worthiness and obedience remain central to the hope of exaltation.

What Latter-day Saints strive for is to be worthy: of the temple, of eternal families, of exaltation. Family is everything — “families can be together forever” is a beloved saying. Their big questions, often unspoken, include: Am I worthy? Have I done enough? Will my family really be together forever? Many quietly carry a heavy sense that they are never quite measuring up. Some struggle with questions about the church’s history.

Why they see the world this way. Many are born into the church and raised in a close, supportive community where faith, family and culture are woven together. Converts are often drawn by the warmth, the clear moral standards and the strong families. Members are taught to seek a spiritual confirmation — a “burning in the bosom” — that the Book of Mormon is true, which makes faith a matter of personal experience rather than evidence. Leaving can mean losing community, family harmony and identity.

What the Bible says to them

There is only one God, who has always been God. Scripture is emphatic: “before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me” (Isaiah 43:10). “From everlasting to everlasting you are God” (Psalm 90:2). God did not become God; he is the eternal, uncreated Creator. “God is spirit” (John 4:24), not an exalted man. And no human being will ever become a god; we are creatures, made to worship him.

Jesus is the eternal God, not our spirit brother. The Son was not created or born as a spirit child; he is the Word who “was in the beginning with God”, through whom “all things were made” (John 1:2–3). He is God the Son, one with the Father in being, not merely in purpose.

Grace means not “after all we can do”. The Bible’s teaching is the opposite of earning: “if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace” (Romans 11:6). We are saved not after all we can do, but because of all Christ has done. Good works and obedience are the fruit of salvation, not the price of it.

You can know you are accepted. Many Latter-day Saints feel they must keep striving for worthiness. The gospel says Christ’s worthiness is given to all who trust him. “For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). Those who believe in the Son “may know” that they have eternal life (1 John 5:13).

God’s word is complete and trustworthy. The Bible has been carefully preserved, and the faith was “once for all delivered to the saints” (Jude 3). Paul warned that even if an angel from heaven preached a different gospel, he should be rejected (Galatians 1:8). We test every claim of new revelation by the Scripture God has already given.

Where to begin

Be a genuine friend. Latter-day Saints value community and kindness. Get to know them, share family life, admire their strengths — their devotion, service and family commitment are real and often admirable.

Define your terms. You will use the same words — God, Jesus, grace, salvation, atonement — with different meanings. Ask, “What do you mean by that?” and explain what you mean. Otherwise you may think you agree when you do not.

Ask about worthiness and assurance. “Do you feel you are worthy of the celestial kingdom?” “How do you know when you have done enough?” Many Latter-day Saints have never been asked, and the honest answer opens the door to grace.

Focus on who God is and on grace. Rather than attacking Joseph Smith or the church’s history, which can make people defensive, show from Scripture who God is and what Christ has done. Share your joy in being accepted by grace alone.

Respect missionaries who knock on your door. They are usually young people far from home. Welcome them, be kind, and ask them to read passages such as Isaiah 43–44 or Ephesians 2 with you. Pray for them.

Walk with those who question. A Latter-day Saint who begins to doubt may lose much. Be patient and faithful, help them find a good church, and remind them that leaving the church is not leaving Jesus — it may be finding him truly for the first time.

6.title: Jewish Friends
6.essay:
Every Christian owes a debt to the Jewish people. Our Scriptures came through them, our Saviour was one of them, and the first church was entirely Jewish. Sharing Christ with Jewish friends is not asking them to leave their story behind, but inviting them to meet the One their story was always about.

Who they are

Jewish people are wonderfully varied. Some are Orthodox, keeping the commandments of the Torah in detail — the Sabbath, the food laws, daily prayer. Others belong to Conservative or Reform synagogues, which adapt tradition to modern life in different degrees. Many are secular: Jewish by family, culture and history, but with little or no belief in God. Some live in Israel, most of the rest in North America and Europe. Never assume you know what a Jewish friend believes; ask.

What unites most Jewish people is a strong sense of belonging to a people with a long, remarkable history. Being Jewish is less about holding a set of beliefs than about identity, family, memory and practice. Judaism is generally more concerned with how you live than with what you believe: doing justice, honouring family, studying, celebrating the festivals, giving to those in need. Many speak of tikkun olam, “repairing the world” — the calling to make the world more just and whole.

Religious Jews treasure the Torah, God’s law given at Sinai, and the covenant between God and Israel. They confess daily the Shema: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). God is one, holy and beyond all images. Sin is real, but people are not seen as fallen or helpless; we have a good inclination and an evil one, and we can choose the good. When we fail, we return to God through repentance, prayer and acts of charity — especially on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement.

Their big questions often concern history and suffering. Where was God in the Holocaust? Why have the Jewish people been hated and persecuted for so long? What does it mean to be chosen? Can God still be trusted? For secular Jews the questions may be more like those of any secular person: Does any of this matter? What do I pass on to my children?

Why they see Christianity as they do. For most Jewish people, Jesus is not a neutral figure. For centuries, people calling themselves Christians accused Jews of killing Christ, forced them into ghettos, expelled them from countries, forced baptisms and massacred communities. The Holocaust happened in the heart of “Christian” Europe. Many Jews have been taught that believing in Jesus means betraying their people and the memory of those who died. They also have theological objections: they understand the Trinity as a departure from the oneness of God, and they argue that Jesus did not do what the Messiah was expected to do — bring peace, rebuild the temple and gather the exiles. A Jewish person who believes in Jesus may face real loss from family and community.

What the Bible says to them

Jesus is the Messiah of Israel. The gospel is not a foreign religion; it is the fulfilment of Israel’s own Scriptures. Jesus was born a Jew, of the line of David, kept the law, worshipped in the temple and taught in the synagogues. He said, “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17). The first believers were Jews who came to see that the promises they had waited for had come true in him.

The prophets point to a suffering Messiah. Many Jewish readers expect a Messiah who will reign in glory. But the prophets also speak of one who would suffer for others. Isaiah 53 describes a servant who “was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). Psalm 22 describes a righteous sufferer whose hands and feet are pierced. Christians believe Jesus came first to suffer and will come again to reign — both strands of prophecy fulfilled in one person.

God promised a new covenant. Through Jeremiah God promised a day when he would write his law on his people’s hearts and “remember their sin no more” (Jeremiah 31:31–34). The covenant at Sinai could not change hearts; Israel’s history shows that again and again. Jesus said at the Last Supper, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20).

Atonement requires a sacrifice. The Torah teaches that “it is the blood that makes atonement by the life” (Leviticus 17:11). Since the temple was destroyed in AD 70, there have been no sacrifices, and rabbinic Judaism has taught that repentance, prayer and charity take their place. The New Testament says that the sacrifices always pointed to one perfect sacrifice: Jesus, the Lamb of God, who offered himself once for all (Hebrews 10:12).

God is one — and has made himself known. Christians confess the Shema too. The Trinity is not three gods; it is the one God revealed as Father, Son and Spirit. Even in the Hebrew Scriptures there are hints of this richness within God’s oneness: the Angel of the LORD who speaks as God, the Spirit of God, the Son whom the nations must honour (Psalm 2:12).

God has not forgotten Israel. Paul, a Jew, said he had “great sorrow and unceasing anguish” in his heart for his people (Romans 9:2), and longed for their salvation. He taught that God’s promises to Israel stand, and the gospel is “to the Jew first” (Romans 1:16). Christians must never speak of Jewish people with contempt; we are wild branches grafted into Israel’s olive tree (Romans 11:17–18).

Where to begin

Begin with humility. Acknowledge the history. If a Jewish friend brings up the church’s persecution of Jews, do not get defensive. Agree that it was evil and that it betrayed Jesus, who was himself Jewish. Your friend needs to know that you love them and respect their people.

Ask about their story and practice. What does being Jewish mean to you? Does your family keep the Sabbath or the festivals? What do you believe about God? Show interest in Passover, Yom Kippur or the Sabbath, and if invited, go. Learn before you speak.

Read the Hebrew Scriptures together. Many Jewish people know their own Scriptures less well than they would like. Ask what they make of Isaiah 53 or Jeremiah 31. Avoid speaking of the “Old” Testament as though it were outdated; it is Scripture, and Christ is found throughout it. Then show how the New Testament reads these passages.

Introduce Jesus the Jew. Matthew’s Gospel, written with Jewish readers in mind, is a natural place to start. Point out how Jesus fulfils the hopes of Israel. Many Jewish people are surprised to find how Jewish Jesus was.

Be sensitive to what faith may cost. A Jewish person who comes to believe in Jesus may face rejection by family. Do not rush or pressure them. Be a faithful friend. If possible, introduce them to Jewish believers in Jesus, who can show that faith in the Messiah does not mean ceasing to be Jewish.

Pray, and wait. Many Jewish people come to faith slowly. The apostle Paul himself was converted from deep opposition. Love, pray, and trust the God who keeps his promises.

7.title: Muslim Friends
7.essay:
Muslims make up nearly a quarter of the world’s population, and many now live as our neighbours, colleagues and classmates. Many are devout, take God seriously and are willing to talk about him. That is a great opportunity — if we come with understanding, respect and love.

Who they are

Islam means “submission” to God, and a Muslim is “one who submits”. Muslims believe in one God, Allah (the Arabic word for God, also used by Arabic-speaking Christians), who is almighty, merciful and utterly unlike his creation. God has sent prophets to every people, including Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David and Jesus. The last and greatest prophet is Muhammad, who lived in Arabia in the seventh century and received the Qur’an, which Muslims believe is God’s final, perfect word.

Islam is a way of life as much as a set of beliefs. Its five pillars are the confession of faith (“There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God”), prayer five times a day, giving to the poor, fasting during the month of Ramadan, and the pilgrimage to Mecca once in a lifetime for those who can. Islamic law (sharia) gives guidance for prayer, food, family, business and much else. There are two main branches, Sunni (the large majority) and Shia, and Muslims differ widely in how strictly they practise. Some are deeply devout; others are cultural Muslims who rarely pray.

Muslims hold Jesus (Isa) in high honour. The Qur’an teaches that he was born of a virgin, worked miracles, was a great prophet and the Messiah, and will return. But it denies that he is the Son of God, which it regards as making a partner for God, the gravest sin (shirk). Most Muslims believe that Jesus was not crucified; God took him to heaven and someone else died in his place. They believe the Bible was originally God’s word but has been corrupted over time.

What Muslims strive for is to please God and to enter paradise. On the Day of Judgment, it is commonly believed, a person’s good and bad deeds will be weighed. No one can be sure of the outcome; it depends on God’s will. Honour, family, community and modesty matter greatly. Many Muslims in the West feel caught between cultures and misunderstood, sometimes treated with suspicion because of terrorism committed in Islam’s name, which most Muslims condemn.

Their big questions often include: Have I done enough to be accepted by God? How can I be sure of paradise? Why does God seem so distant? How can I keep my faith in a secular society? And they may ask Christians, sincerely: How can you believe God has a son? How can God die? Why do you think you can live as you like because Jesus died for you?

Why they see the world this way. Islam arose in the seventh century in a setting of tribal polytheism, and Muhammad’s message of the one God was a call away from idolatry. The Christianity he encountered was divided and sometimes confused, and the Qur’an seems to misunderstand the Trinity as Father, Mother (Mary) and Son. Since then, the Crusades, colonialism and modern conflicts have left a deep sense that the “Christian West” is hostile to Islam. For many Muslims, leaving Islam would mean betraying family and community, and in some countries it carries serious danger.

What the Bible says to them

God is love — and makes himself known. Islam stresses God’s greatness and transcendence; he is known through his will, not personally. The Bible agrees that God is great beyond imagining, but it also says that “God is love” (1 John 4:8), and that love requires someone to love. Within the one God, the Father has loved the Son from eternity. The Trinity is not three gods, as Muslims often think, but the one God who is love in himself. And this God has come near: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

God is both just and merciful. Muslims rightly believe God is just and will judge. But how can a just God forgive sinners without ignoring sin? In Islam, God may simply forgive whom he wills. The Bible shows a God who is “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). At the cross, justice and mercy meet: sin is punished, and sinners are forgiven, because Christ took their place.

The cross is history, and the centre. The crucifixion of Jesus is one of the best-attested facts of ancient history, recorded by Christian, Jewish and Roman sources. And it was no accident or defeat: Jesus foretold it and went to it willingly. “The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). This connects with something Muslims know: the feast of Eid al-Adha remembers God providing a ram in place of Abraham’s son (Genesis 22). Jesus is the sacrifice God provides.

Assurance is a gift. No Muslim can be sure they have done enough. The gospel offers what no system of good works can: certainty. “I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13). Salvation rests not on our record but on Christ’s.

God is a Father who runs. Jesus’ parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15) shows a father who, contrary to every expectation of honour, runs to embrace his returning son. Many Muslims are deeply moved by this picture of God’s welcoming love.

God’s word has been preserved. The Qur’an itself speaks respectfully of the Torah, the Psalms and the Gospel (Injil) as God’s revelation. The manuscript evidence shows that the Bible we have is substantially what was written long before Muhammad. If God is able to preserve his word, as Muslims believe of the Qur’an, he was able to preserve the earlier Scriptures too.

Where to begin

Build genuine friendship. Hospitality is central in Muslim cultures. Accept invitations, share meals (being thoughtful about food: no pork or alcohol), visit during Eid, ask about Ramadan. Many Muslims in the West have never been inside a Christian home.

Talk about God openly. Unlike many secular people, devout Muslims are often glad to talk about faith. Ask them about their prayers, their beliefs, what they hope for. Share how you pray and what God means to you. Do not be embarrassed to speak of Jesus.

Show respect. Never mock Muhammad, the Qur’an or Muslim practices. Treat your Bible with visible respect — Muslims honour their holy book and may be shocked if you put a Bible on the floor. Dress and behave modestly. Respect matters, and it earns a hearing.

Ask questions about assurance and forgiveness. “Do you know if God will accept you on the last day?” “How does God forgive sin and still remain just?” These questions open the way to the gospel more naturally than debate.

Read the Gospels together. Many Muslims are curious to read the Injil for themselves. Luke or John is a good start. Let them see Jesus — his authority, his miracles, his forgiveness of sins, his death and resurrection — and ask what they make of him.

Explain the Trinity carefully. Make clear that Christians do not believe in three gods, nor that God had a son physically with Mary. “Son of God” describes an eternal relationship, not biology. Be patient; this takes time.

Count the cost with them. A Muslim who follows Christ may face rejection, loss and even danger. Do not push. Stand by them, pray with them, and connect them with other believers from Muslim backgrounds if you can. Many Muslims who come to faith speak of dreams or visions of Jesus; God often prepares hearts in ways we do not expect. Pray for your Muslim friends regularly, and keep loving them.

8.title: Hindu Friends
8.essay:
Hinduism is not so much one religion as a vast family of beliefs and practices that grew over thousands of years in India. Hindu friends are often deeply spiritual, warm and open to talking about God — and they may happily add Jesus to the gods they already honour. The challenge is to show that Jesus is not one path among many, but the one in whom God has come to us.

Who they are

Most of the world’s Hindus live in India and Nepal, with large communities in Britain, North America, Africa and elsewhere. There is no single founder, creed or authority. Some Hindus worship one god above all — Vishnu, often through his appearances (avatars) as Krishna or Rama, or Shiva, or the goddess Devi. Others honour many gods and goddesses. Many educated Hindus believe that behind all the gods is one ultimate reality, Brahman, and that the gods are different faces of the one divine. A common saying expresses it: truth is one, but the wise call it by many names.

Several ideas run through most forms of Hinduism. Karma is the moral law of cause and effect: every action brings consequences, in this life or the next. Samsara is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth, in which the soul moves from life to life according to its karma. The goal is moksha, liberation from that cycle. Some seek it through knowledge and meditation, realising that the true self (atman) is one with Brahman; others through devoted love for a personal god (bhakti); others through doing one’s duty faithfully (dharma).

For most Hindus, religion is woven into family and community life: the shrine in the home, festivals such as Diwali and Holi, rituals at birth, marriage and death, respect for elders and duty to family. Many are vegetarian, value non-violence and practise hospitality generously. For second-generation Hindus in the West, faith may be more cultural than personal; they may be exploring what their heritage means.

What Hindus strive for is a good life within this world — family, duty, prosperity — and, beyond it, release from the long cycle of rebirth. Their big questions might include: How can I escape the burden of my karma? Will I ever be free? Which god should I worship? Why is there so much suffering? Some feel the weight of countless lives yet to be lived, and wonder whether they will ever do enough to be released.

Why they see the world this way. Hinduism is ancient and deeply tolerant of variety: it has absorbed many traditions over centuries. To most Hindus it seems natural that there are many paths to the divine, and claims that only one way is true seem narrow and arrogant. Jesus is often respected as a great teacher or even an avatar. But Christianity is sometimes associated with British colonial rule and with Western culture, and in parts of India conversion can bring serious social pressure, including being cut off from family and caste.

What the Bible says to them

God is personal, and he made the world. The Bible begins not with an impersonal absolute, but with a personal God who speaks and creates: “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). The world is not illusion (maya) nor part of God; it is his good creation, distinct from him. And you are not a drop that must dissolve into the ocean of the divine; you are a person made to know and love God for ever.

One life, then judgment — and grace. “It is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment” (Hebrews 9:27). There is no cycle of rebirths in which to work off our karma. That sounds frightening, but the gospel brings astonishing good news: we do not have to pay off our moral debt ourselves at all. Karma says we reap exactly what we sow. Grace says Christ has paid what we owe. “By grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works” (Ephesians 2:8–9).

God has come in the flesh — once, for real. Hindu stories tell of gods appearing in many forms. Jesus is different. He is not one appearance among many, but the eternal Son who truly became human, once, in history: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). He did not come only to teach or to destroy evil, but to die for sinners and rise again. And he said plainly, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).

True liberation. Hindus long for moksha, freedom. Jesus offers a better freedom: not escape from existence, but freedom from sin and its guilt, and a new life with God that begins now and lasts for ever. “If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36).

Living water. Many Hindus perform rituals of washing and purification, seeking to be cleansed. Jesus spoke to a woman at a well about water that satisfies for ever: “whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again” (John 4:14). Only he can cleanse the heart.

Where to begin

Enjoy their friendship and hospitality. Hindus are often very hospitable. Accept invitations to meals and festivals (you can share the meal and the celebration while not taking part in worship of idols). Show interest in their family and traditions. Ask what Diwali means to them.

Ask about their beliefs and practice. Which god do you worship? What do you hope for after this life? Do you think you will be reborn? Listen carefully; Hindus vary enormously, and you need to know what your friend actually believes.

Gently clarify Jesus’ uniqueness. Your friend may say, “Jesus is wonderful; I will put his picture beside my other gods.” Thank them for honouring Jesus, but explain kindly that Jesus himself claimed to be the only way to the Father. He does not ask to be added to our lives, but to be Lord of them.

Share the good news of grace. The contrast between karma and grace is often the most powerful point of contact. Many Hindus feel the burden of trying to be good enough. Tell them how Christ has carried your sin and given you peace with God. Use your own story.

Read the Gospels together. Hindus often love stories, and the Gospels are full of them: healings, parables, Jesus’ compassion for outcasts. John’s Gospel, with its images of light, water, bread and life, often speaks powerfully.

Be patient, and pray. Coming to Christ may mean giving up family shrines and facing pressure from relatives. Do not rush. Pray for your friend and their family, and walk with them through whatever it costs.

9.title: Sikh Friends
9.essay:
Sikhism is the world’s fifth-largest religion, with some twenty-five to thirty million followers, most from the Punjab region of India and Pakistan, and large communities in Britain, Canada and the United States. Sikhs are known for their turbans, their hospitality and their courage. They believe in one God and value devotion, honesty and service. They are often open to talking about God — and their own longing for grace offers a remarkable point of contact.

Who they are

Sikhism was founded by Guru Nanak (1469–1539) in the Punjab. Raised in a Hindu family in a region where Islam was also strong, he taught that there is “neither Hindu nor Muslim”, but one God who is beyond all religious divisions. He was followed by nine further Gurus. The tenth, Guru Gobind Singh, founded the Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs, in 1699, and declared that after him the Guru would be the scripture itself, the Guru Granth Sahib, a collection of hymns by the Gurus and others. Sikhs treat it with the deepest reverence, as a living Guru.

Sikhs believe in one God, often called Waheguru (“Wonderful Lord”), who is the Creator, formless, eternal and present everywhere. The opening words of their scripture, the Mool Mantar, describe God as one, the true Name, the Creator, without fear and without hatred, beyond time, unborn and self-existent. God does not take human form; Sikhs reject idol worship and the Hindu idea of avatars.

Like Hindus, Sikhs believe in karma and rebirth. The goal is mukti, liberation from the cycle of rebirth and union with God. The great obstacle is haumai, ego or self-centredness, which separates us from God and shows itself in lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride. The path to God is to become gurmukh, God-centred rather than self-centred, through remembering and meditating on God’s name (naam simran), honest work and sharing with others. Strikingly, Sikh scripture teaches that liberation finally comes through God’s grace (nadar): it is God who must look on us with favour.

Sikh life is marked by equality and service. The gurdwara (place of worship) always has a langar, a free community kitchen where anyone, of any background, is welcome to sit and eat. Seva, selfless service, is central. Initiated Sikhs keep the Five Ks, including uncut hair (often covered by a turban), a small steel bracelet (kara) and a ceremonial sword (kirpan). Sikhs reject the caste system in principle, and have a proud history of courage and defending the oppressed, including much suffering — notably the persecution of 1984 in India.

What Sikhs strive for is a God-centred, honest, generous life, and ultimately union with God. Their big questions might include: How can I overcome my ego? How do I know if God has looked on me with grace? Will I be freed from rebirth? How do I keep my faith and identity in the West?

Why they see the world this way. Sikhism arose as a devotional movement amid Hindu and Muslim traditions, rejecting ritualism, caste and religious division. For Sikhs, faith is bound up with Punjabi identity, family honour and a history of persecution. Many associate Christianity with British colonial rule, and in India conversions are sometimes viewed with suspicion. Leaving the faith can be seen as betraying family, community and history.

What the Bible says to them

The one Creator has made himself known. Christians share the Sikh conviction that there is one God, the Creator, holy and beyond all idols. But the Bible says this God has not remained formless and distant: “No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18). In Jesus, the eternal Word became flesh — not one avatar among many, but God truly with us, once and for all.

The problem of ego — and its cure. Sikhism rightly sees self-centredness as the root of our separation from God. The Bible calls it sin: putting ourselves in God’s place. But it also shows that we cannot cure it by our own effort; meditation and good works cannot remove the guilt of the past or change the heart. God must give us a new heart: “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).

Grace with a face. Sikh scripture teaches that liberation depends on God’s gracious glance. The gospel shows us how God’s grace has come: “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people” (Titus 2:11). In Christ we do not have to wonder whether God looks on us with favour. On the cross, he took our ego, our pride and our sin on himself, so that all who trust him are welcomed.

One life, and eternal life. Instead of the long cycle of rebirth, the Bible teaches one life, followed by judgment — and offers through Christ a sure hope: “whoever believes in the Son has eternal life” (John 3:36). Union with God is not losing ourselves but being known and loved by him for ever.

Service flows from grace. Christians admire the Sikh practice of seva and langar. Jesus himself came “not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). His service is not only an example but the very means of our salvation — and it frees us to serve others out of gratitude rather than to earn favour.

Where to begin

Visit the gurdwara. Sikhs welcome visitors. Cover your head, remove your shoes, and share in the langar. Ask your friend to explain what you see. It is a wonderful way to show respect and begin friendship.

Ask about their faith. What does Waheguru mean to you? How do you overcome ego? What does grace mean in Sikh teaching? Do you know if you will be united with God? Listen carefully; Sikhs vary in practice, from devout Khalsa members to more secular Punjabis.

Build on shared ground. One God, the danger of pride, the importance of honest work, service and equality — these are real points of contact. Then gently show how Jesus fulfils the longings Sikh teaching expresses, especially the longing for grace.

Show respect. Never mock the turban or other articles of faith, and treat the Guru Granth Sahib with respect. Do not assume all Sikhs are Hindus or Muslims; the distinction matters deeply to them.

Share Jesus and his grace. Tell your story of how Christ has dealt with your pride and sin, and given you assurance. Read the Gospels together — Luke’s, with its stories of Jesus welcoming outsiders, or John’s, with its revelation of God made known.

Be patient and loyal. A Sikh who follows Jesus may face pressure from family and community. Walk with them, honour their family, and pray faithfully.

10.title: Buddhist Friends
10.essay:
Buddhism began with one man’s search for an answer to suffering. Today it is the religion of hundreds of millions in Asia — and, in a softer form, an attractive spirituality for many Westerners seeking calm in a restless world. Buddhist friends often understand something many Christians forget: that life in this world is marked by suffering. The gospel speaks to that suffering in a way nothing else can.

Who they are

Buddhism traces back to Siddhartha Gautama, who lived in northern India around the fifth century BC. Raised in luxury as a prince, he encountered sickness, old age and death, left his comfortable life to seek an answer, and after years of searching attained “enlightenment” while meditating. He became the Buddha, “the awakened one”. He did not claim to be a god, and he did not teach about a creator.

The Buddha’s teaching is summed up in the Four Noble Truths: life is marked by suffering and dissatisfaction (dukkha); suffering is caused by craving and attachment; suffering can end; and the way to end it is the Noble Eightfold Path of right understanding, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration. Like Hinduism, Buddhism teaches karma and rebirth. The goal is nirvana, the “blowing out” of craving and the end of the cycle of rebirth. Buddhism also teaches that there is no permanent self: what we call “I” is a changing bundle of experiences.

There are two great traditions. Theravada Buddhism, in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar and Cambodia, stresses individual discipline and meditation, often led by monks. Mahayana Buddhism, in China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam and Tibet, includes the ideal of the bodhisattva, an enlightened being who delays nirvana to help others, and in some forms prayer to Buddhas for help. In practice many Asian Buddhists also honour ancestors and spirits. In the West, many are attracted to a simplified Buddhism focused on meditation, mindfulness and inner peace, often with little interest in rebirth or monks.

What Buddhists strive for is peace: freedom from craving, anxiety and suffering, compassion toward all living things and, ultimately, release. Their big questions are deeply human: Why is there so much suffering? How can I find peace? How can I stop wanting what does not satisfy? What happens when I die? Who am I, really?

Why they see the world this way. Buddhism grew from honest reflection on suffering and impermanence: everything we love changes and passes. For Asian Buddhists, it is woven into national identity and family life, and leaving it may feel like betraying your people and your ancestors. Western Buddhists are often drawn because Buddhism seems peaceful, rational and free of dogma, in contrast to a Christianity they think of as judgmental or out of date. Mindfulness practices are now everywhere, in schools, workplaces and therapy.

What the Bible says to them

Suffering is real — and so is the God who suffers. The Bible takes suffering as seriously as the Buddha did: the whole creation “was subjected to futility” and groans (Romans 8:20–22). But the Bible says more. The world was made good, and suffering came through human rebellion against God. And God has not stayed distant from our pain. In Jesus he entered it: he wept at his friend’s tomb (John 11:35), was rejected, betrayed and crucified. The Buddha sat beneath a tree to escape suffering; Jesus hung on a tree to bear it for us.

Desire is not the enemy — misdirected desire is. Buddhism teaches that craving causes suffering, and so seeks to extinguish desire. Scripture agrees that disordered desires enslave us. But its answer is not to stop desiring, but to desire the right thing: God himself. “You make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy” (Psalm 16:11). Jesus said, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew 5:6). Our hearts are not meant to be emptied but filled.

You are a real person, known and loved. Buddhism teaches that the self is an illusion. The Bible says each person is made by God, in his image, known by name: “Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine” (Isaiah 43:1). Personhood is not a problem to be dissolved but a gift to be redeemed.

Grace, not effort. The Eightfold Path is demanding, and few believe they will reach nirvana in this life. The gospel announces that the way to God is not a path we must walk alone, but a person who has come to carry us: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Jesus offers not the extinction of the self, but forgiveness, new life and peace with God.

A real hope beyond death. Instead of endless rebirth or the blowing out of existence, Christ offers resurrection: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live” (John 11:25). And one day God will make all things new, wiping away every tear (Revelation 21:4). Suffering will not merely be escaped; it will be undone.

Where to begin

Start with what you share. Talk honestly about suffering, loss and longing. Buddhists value honesty about pain; Christians should not pretend life is easy. Ask: What drew you to Buddhism? How do you deal with suffering? What does peace mean to you?

Listen for the kind of Buddhism they hold. An elderly Thai Buddhist who visits the temple and honours the monks, and a young Westerner who practises mindfulness, have very different beliefs. Ask what they actually believe about rebirth, the self and the goal of life.

Show them Jesus who suffers with us. The cross speaks powerfully to people who think deeply about suffering. Explain that God himself took suffering on himself to free us, and that because of the resurrection suffering does not have the last word.

Offer rest, not another path. Many Buddhists, especially in the West, feel the strain of striving for calm. Share how Christ gives rest to the weary, because salvation is his gift rather than our achievement. Share your own experience of peace in suffering.

Read and pray together. Suggest reading a Gospel together, perhaps Luke, with its compassion for the poor and suffering. If your friend is open, offer to pray for them in a time of need; many Buddhists are touched to be prayed for, and God often answers.

Be patient and gentle. For Asian Buddhists especially, faith in Christ can mean tension with family and ancestors. Walk with them patiently, honour their family, and trust God to open their eyes.

11.title: The Gospel Conversation
11.essay:
Whoever your friend is — secular or spiritual, Catholic, Witness or Latter-day Saint, Jewish, Muslim, Hindu, Sikh or Buddhist — at some point you will want to talk about Jesus. This last chapter is about how ordinary Christians can do that naturally, clearly and kindly: by praying, listening, asking good questions, sharing their own story and explaining the good news itself.

Pray first, and keep praying

Conversion is the work of God. Only the Spirit can “convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment” (John 16:8). So the first step in any gospel conversation is prayer — for the person by name, for opportunities, and for courage and wisdom when they come. Paul asked the Colossians to pray “that God may open to us a door for the word” (Colossians 4:3). Ask God to open doors, and watch for them.

Listen well

Most people are rarely listened to. When we listen carefully — to their story, their questions, their hurts — we honour them and learn how the gospel might speak to them. Jesus asked questions constantly: “What do you want me to do for you?” (Mark 10:51). Be genuinely curious. Do not rush to answer; first understand.

Ask good questions

Good questions open doors that statements cannot. Some simple ones: What do you believe about God? What gives your life meaning? Have you ever read the Gospels? What do you think happens when we die? If you could know God personally, would you want to? Then follow up: Why do you think that? How did you come to see it that way? Questions invite people to think, rather than to defend themselves.

Share your story

You do not need to be a theologian to tell what Christ has done for you. The man born blind could say only, “One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see” (John 9:25) — and it was enough. Practise telling your story briefly: what your life was like, how you came to know Christ, and what difference he makes now. Keep it honest, and keep the focus on Jesus rather than on yourself.

Explain the gospel clearly

At some point, your friend needs to hear the gospel itself. Paul summed it up: “that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). It helps to have a simple outline in mind, such as these four words.

God. God made us and the world, and he made us to know him, love him and enjoy him for ever. He is holy, just and loving.

Sin. We have all turned away from God and gone our own way. “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). Sin separates us from God and deserves his judgment, and we cannot fix it by our own efforts.

Christ. God sent his Son, Jesus, who lived the perfect life we have not lived, died on the cross in our place to take the punishment our sins deserve, and rose from the dead. “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Response. God calls us to turn from our sin and trust in Jesus. Everyone who does so is forgiven, made a child of God and given eternal life. “If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans 10:9).

Use your own words, and connect the gospel with what you have learned about your friend: their longing for meaning, their guilt, their fear of death, their weariness of striving.

Answer questions honestly

People will raise objections: suffering, other religions, the reliability of the Bible, science, hell, hypocrisy in the church. Do not panic. Take the question seriously, and answer as best you can. If you do not know, say so — and offer to find out and come back. Often the question behind the question matters most: a question about suffering may come from a painful loss. Answer the person, not just the argument. And remember Paul’s counsel: “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Colossians 4:6).

Invite, and keep walking with them

At the right time, invite your friend to take a next step: to read a Gospel with you, to come to church, to join a course such as Christianity Explored, or to put their trust in Christ. Do not pressure, but do not be afraid to ask. Some will say yes; many will say not yet; some will say no. Keep loving them whatever their answer. Faith often grows slowly, through many conversations.

Trust God with the results

Evangelism is not a sales technique, and success is not measured by how many people we persuade. It is faithfulness: praying, loving and speaking. “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). You may plant a seed that another will water and God will bring to life years later. That frees you to be faithful, joyful and unafraid — and to keep going.
